idiom_name: Spring @Service + @Transactional with the kotlin-spring all-open plugin
implementation_notes: The service is a @Service class and the transaction boundary is @Transactional, applied by Spring's proxy. Kotlin classes and member functions are final by default, so the kotlin-spring (all-open) compiler plugin opens Spring beans for subclass-based proxies; without it, application-context startup fails when Spring cannot create the proxy rather than making the annotation silently effective. A suspend function also needs transaction support compatible with coroutine execution; an imperative proxy alone is not a substitute for a coroutine-aware manager or an explicit suspend transaction.
pitfalls: Wrong move: omit the kotlin-spring all-open plugin for a proxied service; failure: Spring cannot create the subclass-based proxy and bean startup fails; instead: enable the plugin or explicitly open the proxied class and method.

Wrong move: assume imperative @Transactional automatically covers arbitrary suspend execution; failure: the transaction context may not follow coroutine suspension; instead: use a coroutine-aware/reactive transaction manager or an explicit suspendTransaction block.
Injecting through a secondary constructor with default values confuses the container; prefer a primary constructor with val properties.

variants.name: Suspend use-case service over Exposed transactions
variants.implementation_notes: A coroutine-native realization: the service is a class of suspend functions and the transaction boundary is Exposed's suspendTransaction (successor of newSuspendedTransaction), which supplies a JdbcTransaction receiver to the suspend block and rolls back on any throwable; repositories are suspend functions, but JDBC remains blocking, so confine the database work to an appropriate IO dispatcher. Choose it when the stack is coroutine-based and the transaction should be an explicit block rather than an annotation, because an imperative proxy-based @Transactional boundary does not by itself provide coroutine-aware transaction context.
pitfalls: suspendTransaction catches all throwables (including cancellation) to guarantee rollback; re-throw cancellation when the caller must observe it.
Blocking JDBC calls inside a coroutine without withContext(Dispatchers.IO) starve the default dispatcher.
A coroutine launched with a different context/job runs outside the transaction even if it was started inside the block.
